papers.note: Reaches 100 percent jailbreak success across the major frontier models using simple adaptive search.
papers.title: Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers discovered that even the most advanced AI chatbots with built-in safety features can be tricked into ignoring their guidelines using relatively straightforward techniques. By adding carefully crafted text snippets to requests, attackers achieved a perfect success rate against every major commercial AI model tested. This matters because it reveals that current safety protections are weaker than assumed, highlighting the need for better defenses before these systems become more widely deployed.
papers.explain_business: Leading AI providers have safety systems that can be completely bypassed using simple, reproducible methods. Organizations deploying these models should recognize that published safety benchmarks may not reflect real-world robustness. This informs procurement decisions and risk assessments: current guardrails require substantial improvement before handling sensitive applications. The reproducible nature of these attacks means competitors or malicious actors can easily replicate bypasses, making immediate investment in robust defense mechanisms a strategic priority.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study demonstrates adaptive jailbreaking via random search optimization on model logprobs. For models exposing logprobs, researchers designed adversarial templates and appended optimized suffixes targeting high probability of unsafe tokens like 'Sure'. For models without logprob access, transfer attacks and prefilling exploits achieved equivalent success. Critical finding: adaptation to each model's architecture and API characteristics proved essential. They achieved 100% success across GPT-4o, Llama-3, Gemma, Claude variants, and 10+ other frontier models, including R2D2 specifically adversarially trained against prior GCG attacks.

papers.note: Survey of jailbreaking, data poisoning and personal-information leakage against language models, with the defences proposed so far. The natural companion to our AI Security section.
papers.title: Security and Privacy Challenges of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models like ChatGPT are powerful AI tools used for writing, translation, and answering questions. However, researchers have discovered they face three major security problems: attackers can trick them into harmful outputs, bad actors can corrupt their training data, and they can accidentally reveal personal information about people. This survey examines these threats across real-world applications like healthcare and education, and reviews ways to protect these systems. Understanding these risks matters because LLMs are increasingly used to make important decisions.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models face significant security and privacy risks that could damage reputation, violate regulations, and compromise user data. This survey documents three critical threat types affecting healthcare, education, and transportation applications. For decision makers, it clarifies the current vulnerability landscape and what defenses exist today, enabling informed choices about deployment readiness, risk tolerance, and required safeguards before integrating these tools into customer-facing or sensitive operations.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey systematically examines three attack vectors against large language models: jailbreaking techniques that circumvent safety guidelines, data poisoning that corrupts model training, and extraction attacks exposing personally identifiable information. The authors assess vulnerability severity, categorize emerging attack methods, and evaluate existing defense strategies across multiple domains including transportation, education, and healthcare. The work identifies specific research gaps and proposes directions for developing more robust protective mechanisms, providing practitioners with a comprehensive threat landscape and current state of defense techniques.

papers.note: Shows reasoning models are not safer than their base models, and releases the first chain of thought safety training set.
papers.title: SafeChain: Safety of Language Models with Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities

papers.note: Self replicating prompts spread between agents like a virus, the key risk when clients deploy multi agent systems.
papers.title: Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems

papers.note: Reverse engineers commercial chatbot defences using timing side channels, a red team method with real disclosure history.
papers.title: MASTERKEY: Automated Jailbreaking of Large Language Model Chatbots
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers discovered that popular AI chatbots can be tricked into saying things they are designed not to say. The study shows how attackers can craft special prompts that bypass safety features, causing the AI to generate harmful content that violates its guidelines. This matters because it reveals security weaknesses in widely-used AI systems that people rely on, highlighting the need for better protections.
papers.explain_business: This research identifies a critical vulnerability in deployed AI chatbot systems where attackers can systematically extract harmful outputs despite implemented safety measures. Organizations deploying large language models must recognize that existing defenses are bypassable and evaluate their security posture accordingly. The findings inform decisions about deployment contexts, additional oversight layers, and prioritization of improved defense mechanisms before wider commercial rollout.
papers.explain_practitioner: The research demonstrates automated jailbreaking techniques that exploit timing side channels to reverse-engineer chatbot defenses. The methodology involves crafting adversarial prompts that manipulate input in strategic ways to circumvent safeguards. The key result is that commercial LLM chatbots can be reliably compromised to produce moderated or blocked outputs, with the findings responsibly disclosed following established vulnerability reporting practices.

papers.note: Non expert persuasion techniques beat algorithmic attacks at over 92 percent success, which widens the realistic threat population.
papers.title: How Johnny Can Persuade LLMs to Jailbreak Them: Rethinking Persuasion to Challenge AI Safety by Humanizing LLMs
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers discovered that everyday persuasion techniques, like those people naturally use in conversation, can trick advanced AI systems into ignoring their safety guidelines over 92 percent of the time. Unlike previous attacks requiring technical expertise, anyone can use these methods during normal interactions. This matters because it shows AI safety depends not just on defending against complex hacking attempts, but also protecting against how ordinary people naturally talk to these systems.
papers.explain_business: Current AI safety measures focus on technical defenses but are largely ineffective against persuasion-based attacks that ordinary users can execute without special knowledge. Organizations deploying large language models face substantial risk from routine user interactions, not just sophisticated hackers. This finding requires companies to reconsider safety architectures fundamentally, as conventional defensive approaches do not adequately address how social influence techniques can compromise system reliability and trustworthiness.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study applies established social science persuasion principles to create prompts that jailbreak LLMs automatically. Researchers developed a taxonomy of persuasion techniques and used it to generate adversarial prompts targeting Llama-2-7b-Chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4. The persuasion-based approach achieved over 92 percent success rates across all tested risk categories, outperforming algorithm-focused attacks. Existing defense mechanisms showed significant gaps, indicating that current safeguards are inadequate against this class of attacks.

papers.note: First taxonomy joining input level exploits to protocol level vulnerabilities, cross mapped to CVE and NIST NVD.
papers.title: From Prompt Injections to Protocol Exploits: Threats in LLM-Powered AI Agents Workflows

papers.note: Principled agent design patterns with provable injection resistance, the constructive counterpart to the attack literature.
papers.title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections

papers.note: Breaks the LLM as judge pattern that many evaluation and RLAIF pipelines depend on.
papers.title: Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security
papers.explain_beginner: Companies increasingly use AI systems to judge which answers are best. This paper shows that attackers can sneak hidden instructions into their responses to trick the judging AI into picking their answer every time, regardless of quality. Researchers created an automated attack method that finds exactly what to hide in a response to manipulate the judge. They tested defenses but found them ineffective, revealing a serious vulnerability in how AI evaluation systems work today.
papers.explain_business: Organizations using AI judges to evaluate responses face a critical vulnerability. Attackers can manipulate the judging process to force selection of their content by embedding invisible instructions in responses. This undermines systems that automate quality assessment, recommendation ranking, and AI model training through feedback. Current protective measures fail to stop sophisticated attacks. Organizations should pause reliance on LLM judges for high-stakes decisions until stronger safeguards are developed, or implement additional human review layers for critical evaluation tasks.
papers.explain_practitioner: This work presents JudgeDeceiver, an optimization-based prompt injection attack targeting LLM-as-a-Judge systems. The authors formulate the attack as an optimization problem and employ gradient-based methods to discover adversarial sequences that, when embedded in candidate responses, consistently cause the judge model to select them across diverse queries. Evaluation demonstrates superior effectiveness compared to manual prompt injection and jailbreak baselines. The attack succeeds in three application domains: LLM-based search, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, and tool selection. Tested defenses including perplexity-based filtering prove insufficient against the attack.

papers.note: Covers Model Context Protocol tool poisoning and RAG poisoning, and maps defences to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025.
papers.title: Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models and AI Agent Systems: A Comprehensive Review of Vulnerabilities, Attack Vectors, and Defense Mechanisms
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines a major security problem with AI language models: attackers can trick them into ignoring their instructions and misbehaving. As these AI systems become more integrated into real applications, new attack methods have emerged, especially through connected tools and external data sources. The researchers found that attackers can manipulate AI responses with surprising ease, and they propose a multi-layered defense strategy to protect against these threats.
papers.explain_business: Prompt injection attacks pose substantial risk to deployed AI systems, with documented severe incidents like remote code execution vulnerabilities and credential theft. Minimal attack effort achieves high success rates, particularly when data sources are involved. Organizations implementing AI agents must adopt comprehensive, layered security approaches aligned with OWASP standards rather than relying on single defenses. This represents an ongoing architectural challenge requiring continuous monitoring and evolving protection strategies as threat vectors expand.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive review analyzes prompt injection vulnerabilities in LLMs and agent systems from 2023-2025, examining 45 sources and real exploits. It categorizes attack vectors including direct jailbreaking, indirect injection via external content, tool poisoning through MCP, and RAG poisoning demonstrating 90% manipulation success with five documents. Critical incidents documented include CVE-2025-53773 (CVSS 9.6) and credential leakage. The authors propose PALADIN, a five-layer defense framework, and map mitigations to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, identifying fundamental limitations requiring architectural rather than tactical solutions.

papers.note: Bypasses all eight tested defences at over 50 percent success, so any vendor injection defence claim needs adaptive testing.
papers.title: Adaptive Attacks Break Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested eight different security protections designed to stop a specific type of attack on AI assistants that use external tools and information. They found that with clever, adaptive attacks, they could break through every single protection more than half the time. This matters because companies relying on these defenses might think their systems are safer than they actually are, potentially exposing users to harmful manipulation.
papers.explain_business: Current marketed defenses against prompt injection attacks are not as effective as claimed when tested against sophisticated attackers. Any vendor claiming protection against this threat should undergo rigorous adaptive testing to validate their claims. Organizations deploying LLM agents with external tool access should recognize that existing defenses have significant gaps and require additional safeguards or architectural changes before relying on them for security-critical applications.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study evaluated eight defense mechanisms against indirect prompt injection attacks targeting LLM agents with tool integration. Using adaptive attacks tailored to each defense's specific approach, researchers achieved over 50 percent bypass rates across all tested defenses. The key finding is that static defense evaluations are insufficient; adaptive attack testing that evolves based on defense characteristics is necessary to properly assess robustness and identify fundamental vulnerabilities in protection mechanisms.

papers.note: Extends the NIST adversarial machine learning taxonomy across 88 studies and catalogues defence effectiveness by model.
papers.title: A Systematic Literature Review on LLM Defenses Against Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking: Expanding NIST Taxonomy
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models like ChatGPT can be tricked by carefully written prompts that make them leak secrets, perform unauthorized tasks, or give false information. Researchers reviewed 88 studies on ways to protect against these attacks and organized their findings using a framework from the US government agency NIST. The work identifies different defense strategies, measures how well each one works with different models, and creates a practical guide for developers building safer AI systems.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models face significant security risks from prompt injection attacks that can cause data breaches or system misuse. This research catalogs proven defense strategies with measured effectiveness across different models, enabling technical teams to select appropriate protections based on their specific systems and threat profiles. The standardized framework and open-source solutions identified help companies implement defenses efficiently while reducing security vulnerabilities and potential liability from AI system compromise.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review analyzed 88 peer-reviewed studies on prompt injection defenses and extended NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy with additional defense categories. The authors documented quantitative effectiveness metrics for mitigation strategies across specific LLMs and attack datasets, cataloguing which defenses are open-source and model-agnostic. By establishing standardized terminology and taxonomy grounded in NIST's framework, the work provides a structured foundation for comparing defense mechanisms and enables reproducible research for developing more robust LLM security solutions.
